about: The wire contract of the secrets broker's RFC 8693 token exchange, as its two clients speak it: the Go client of packages/envoy/internal/cipherclient and the TypeScript client of packages/cipher-client.
Each suite reads this one file and replays every exchange below against a stub broker of its own, so neither client's idea of the contract is only its own.

The rule that makes 'one contract' checkable rather than asserted: form, proof.header and proof.claims are the WHOLE of what a request carries. A suite asserts set equality, not containment, so a field one client starts sending without an entry here fails that client's own test, and a field added here fails the other client's test until it sends it too. expect.token is read the same way: it is the whole of what a client may take from an answer, so a client that starts reading another member of the answer fails until this file names it.
A value of the form ${name} is a placeholder each suite substitutes or checks by shape; placeholders names them. Everything else is literal and compared byte for byte.

There is no audience parameter: the broker's exchange has none. A subject token's own audience is what names the broker it may be spent at (BROKER_EXCHANGE_K8S_AUDIENCE, BROKER_GOOGLE_OIDC_AUDIENCE, BROKER_SIGNIN_DEVICE_AUDIENCE), and a client that posted one would be posting a field the broker does not read.

placeholders.${subject_token}: the token the exchange's subject source answered at this trade
placeholders.${actor_token}: the token the actor source answered at this trade
placeholders.${session}: the session name the client was configured with, as the entry's session names it
placeholders.${projects}: the projects the client was configured with, as the entry's projects names them, joined by one space
placeholders.${token_endpoint}: the stub broker's own origin followed by endpoint.path, with no query and no fragment
placeholders.${jti}: a value this request alone carries: non-empty, and never equal to another request's
placeholders.${iat}: the time the proof was signed, in whole seconds, within a minute of the suite's clock
placeholders.${public_jwk}: the public half of the client's own key: an EC P-256 JWK carrying x and y and no d member at all

exchanges.name: a pod trades its projected Kubernetes service-account token
exchanges.about: The identity a pod already holds, read from the file its runtime mounts and read again at every renewal, since the kubelet rewrites it in place.

exchanges.name: a machine trades its Google identity token
exchanges.about: A Compute Engine machine's own identity token, asked of its metadata server with format=full and fetched through no proxy. An entry that fixes the session leaves the client naming none.

exchanges.name: a trade that wants no launcher credential
exchanges.about: A caller that wants a Dispatch access token and nothing else sends launcher_credential=false, and the broker mints or moves no launcher credential for it: the answer carries no credential_id and no credential_expires_at, and the client reads the credential it was given as none. Every TypeScript client's machine trade is this one, since none of them enrols a session or reads a secret and a machine's key is one process's and one session's, so a trade that asked would leave a launcher_credentials row and a token_login audit row behind for each of them. The parameter is absent from every other entry here because an absent parameter asks: that is what agent-secrets, the helper and a person's sign-in send, a TypeScript client's trade of a sign-in included, since the broker refuses a person's trade that declines, and what a client written before this parameter sends.

exchanges.name: a person trades their sign-in with the machine as the actor
exchanges.about: The one request that carries two tokens: the person's own Google identity token from the device grant, and the machine's as the actor token, under a type of its own because what it proves is which box the person is asking from.

exchanges.name: a person's session trades their sign-in naming its projects
exchanges.about: A session started with AGENT_SECRETS_PROJECTS names the projects it works on, and its person's trade sends them as the broker's projects parameter: the keys sorted, each once, joined by one space. The broker mints a token naming them only when Dispatch says the person may see each one. A trade naming no project sends no projects parameter at all, which is every other entry here; a machine trading for itself never sends one, since its entry decides its project.

exchanges.name: a device login trades its machine login's access token
exchanges.about: A machine with no platform identity of its own, such as a person's laptop, logs in once through the broker's device grant and keeps that login (AGENT_SECRETS_MACHINE_IDENTITY=device-login). It presents the access token the login holds under RFC 8693's own access_token type, with no actor: the login already names the person who approved it. The proof is signed with the login's own key, since the access token is bound to it. The trade names the projects its session works on, and sends no launcher_credential parameter: a trade of a machine login's token mints no launcher credential, so the answer names none.

exchanges.name: the broker refuses the identity
exchanges.about: An identity no entry lists, a revoked sign-in, a token of the wrong audience: a refusal no retry can cure. The client stops with a plain error carrying what the broker said, and holds no token.

body.error_description: no entry lists the account this token names

expect.error_contains: no entry lists the account this token names

exchanges.name: the broker's token endpoint is out of bucket
exchanges.about: The first of the five refusals a later trade may be answered differently: the endpoint spends a bucket per source address, and a bucket refills. A client with nothing live in hand still fails the call, and says what the broker said; a client holding a live token keeps writing with it instead (expect.permanent is false).

body.error_description: too many token requests; try again later

expect.error_contains: too many token requests; try again later

exchanges.name: the broker has no registration for this pod's session yet
exchanges.about: A pod trades under a session name its deployment registers for it, and its trade can reach the broker before that registration does: its daemon registers at the claim, a session's watch at the pod's creation, and either can be down for minutes. The broker refuses it invalid_grant with an error_description beginning pod_session_not_registered:, a refusal of the broker's state that a later trade cures, so neither client reads it as final (expect.permanent is false). A pod's trade sends no projects field: its entry decides its project. The Go client's Token answers the refusal and its Run trades again; the TypeScript client's token() trades again until its caller stops waiting, and then answers it.

body.error_description: pod_session_not_registered: No registration says this pod may write under the session name 'example-worker-session'. A pod writes under a session name its deployment registered for it.

expect.error_contains: pod_session_not_registered: No registration says this pod may write under the session name 'example-worker-session'.

exchanges.name: a daemon other than the one the session name is bound to registered this pod
exchanges.about: A session name belongs for good to the daemon that first registered it, and a pod trades under it only when that daemon registered the pod. A pod another daemon registered under the name, or one registered under a name bound to no daemon, is refused invalid_grant with an error_description beginning session_name_not_this_registrars:. No later trade cures it, since only the holding daemon's registration of the pod would admit it, or, under a name bound to no daemon, a registration that binds the name to the pod's registrar, so both clients read it as final (expect.permanent is true), unlike the pod_session_not_registered: refusal above: the Go client's Token answers the refusal and its Run stops on it, and the TypeScript client's token() ends its retry loop and answers it, dropping any token in hand.

body.error_description: session_name_not_this_registrars: The session name 'example-worker-session' belongs to another daemon: a pod trades only under a session name the daemon that registered it holds.

expect.error_contains: session_name_not_this_registrars: The session name 'example-worker-session' belongs to another daemon: a pod trades only under a session name the daemon that registered it holds.

exchanges.name: the broker refuses this moment's DPoP proof
exchanges.about: The broker answers invalid_dpop_proof to a proof whose iat is outside its 60 s skew window, which is what a process started before NTP has corrected the host's clock signs. It is no judgement of the identity, so it is not a refusal a client stops on: one that dropped the token in hand here would fail every Dispatch and listener call until something restarted it, while the next trade after the correction succeeds. The broker's other DPoP refusal, use_dpop_nonce, is read the same way: each client already retries one once with the nonce the answer carried, and one that reaches the caller is an answer that carried no nonce, or a nonce the broker then refused in turn.

body.error_description: the proof's iat is outside the broker's skew window

expect.error_contains: the proof's iat is outside the broker's skew window

exchanges.name: Dispatch holds the person a sign-in names
exchanges.about: The broker answers membership_held to a trade that names a person whom Dispatch holds until they sign in again: Google refused their Dispatch sign-in, or no refresh has confirmed them for 24 hours. A hold revokes nothing, and the person's next Dispatch sign-in, or the next refresh that confirms them, ends it, so it is not a refusal a client stops on (expect.permanent is false): each client keeps the identity it trades, a person's sign-in on the machine included, and trades again, and the first trade after the release is served with no new sign-in, machine login or approval.

body.error_description: ada@example.com's credentials are held by Dispatch; they work again when ada@example.com signs in to Dispatch, or when Dispatch can confirm ada@example.com with Google again

expect.error_contains: ada@example.com's credentials are held by Dispatch; they work again when ada@example.com signs in to Dispatch, or when Dispatch can confirm ada@example.com with Google again

exchanges.name: Dispatch holds the person a sign-in names, behind Identity-Aware Proxy
exchanges.about: An Identity-Aware Proxy deployment's broker (BROKER_HOLD_REQUIRES_DEADLINE) answers membership_held in the Workspace Directory's words: Dispatch holds the person because the Directory no longer confirms their account, and its next active answer, not a sign-in, ends the hold. It is the same refusal as the row before, so it is not one a client stops on either (expect.permanent is false), and each client prints its words whole for the person the trade names.

body.error_description: Google's Workspace Directory no longer confirms ada@example.com; their credentials work again once it does

expect.error_contains: Google's Workspace Directory no longer confirms ada@example.com; their credentials work again once it does

exchanges.name: an answer that carries a refresh token
exchanges.about: This grant issues none: a renewal is a fresh subject token traded again. A client that kept one would hold a credential the contract says is never minted, so an answer carrying one is refused.

exchanges.name: an answer of a token type that is not DPoP
exchanges.about: Every token this grant mints is bound to the key the caller proved. A bearer token would be one a copy of the answer could spend, so the client refuses it rather than presenting it.
